reader.title: Lynching of William Nicholson
bases: Every report says William Nicholson was 'lynched' for murder at Saunders Station, N.M., and one quoted item says by 'a mob' (A2, A6, A7, A18).

Three separately datelined dispatches say Nicholson was lynched for murder or for 'killing a man without provocation' (A2, A6, A7), but none describes the killers; only a San Francisco Examiner line quoted a month later says 'a mob' (A18), with no number or detail.

A Denver special (A2), a Las Vegas dispatch relayed from Chicago (A6) and a Santa Fe dispatch (A7) agree that Nicholson was lynched at Saunders Station for a killing, though each gives the fact in a single line.

summary.text: The lynching of William Nicholson took place at Saunders Station, a stop on the Southern Pacific in New Mexico Territory, on the night of Thursday, October 6, 1881.
He was accused of murder, specifically of "killing a man without provocation."
The killing reached the national press only as a one-line addendum to reports of a double lynching at Socorro the same night.
The dispatches that carried Nicholson's name were chiefly about Socorro, where two men known as Clark, alias "Butch," and "Frenchy," accused of robbing a commission house, were hanged.
A Santa Fe dispatch attributed those hangings to a "Vigilance Committee" but linked no group to the killing at Saunders Station.
According to a special dispatch to the Denver Republican, "William Nicholson was also lynched at Saunders station, N. M., for murder."
A separate dispatch from Las Vegas, New Mexico, relayed through Chicago, gave the same fact in nearly the same words.
The Santa Fe dispatch added that the station lay on the Southern Pacific and that Nicholson was lynched "the same night" as the Socorro hangings, for "killing a man without provocation."
None of these reports named the man Nicholson was accused of killing, described the lynchers or their number, or said how he was killed.
Only a line from the San Francisco Examiner, quoted a month later, said he was "lynched by a mob."
No report gave his race.
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage.

In November the Concord Sun of North Carolina, as reprinted in the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic, wrote, "We recently gave the rumor that William Nicholson, a refugee from this county, had been killed out West."
The Sun then quoted the Examiner's line as confirmation, though nothing beyond the shared name connected the two men in its report.

The Denver Republican's special was the version most widely reprinted, appearing on October 8 and 9 in the Cheyenne Daily Leader, the Gold Hill Daily News, the Chicago Daily Tribune, the Daily Los Angeles Herald, the Richmond Daily Dispatch and the Knoxville Daily Chronicle.
Later papers, including the Iowa Plain Dealer, the Dallas Weekly Herald and the Huntsville Gazette, ran it in news-brief columns between October 13 and 15.
Typesetting garbled the place as "Standish Station," "Staunder's Station" and "Staurden's Station," and the name once as "Niehelson."
Headlines framed the item within the Socorro story, as "Lynch Law in New Mexico," "Three Men Lynched in New Mexico," "Desperadoes Lynched" and "Judge Lynch."
The papers offered no comment on Nicholson's killing beyond the accusation against him.
Only the North Carolina item treated him as a person of interest in his own right, as a former local man.

accounts.label: Denver Republican special
accounts.gist: After reporting the Socorro lynching of two robbers, adds that Nicholson 'was also lynched at Saunders station, N. M., for murder.'

accounts.label: Las Vegas dispatch via Chicago
accounts.gist: Describes the Socorro hanging and placard, then states Nicholson was lynched at Saunders' Station for murder.

accounts.label: Santa Fe dispatch
accounts.gist: Places Saunders Station on the Southern Pacific and says Nicholson was lynched the same Thursday night for killing a man without provocation.

accounts.label: San Francisco Examiner, quoted by the Concord Sun
accounts.gist: Says Nicholson was 'lynched by a mob, for murder'; the Sun identifies him with a refugee from its own county.

framing.detail: Papers from Cheyenne to Richmond ran the Denver wire's single sentence on Nicholson beneath the Socorro story, under headlines such as 'Three Men Lynched in New Mexico' and 'Judge Lynch.'
The Santa Fe dispatch, headed 'Three Men Lynched', added the accusation that he killed 'a man without provocation' without comment.
The Concord Sun treated the item as news of a local man, confirming an earlier rumor of his death.

conflicts.note: Spelling and typesetting variants of one place name in the same wire; the first form is the most common and appears in all three independent dispatches.
